-

Student-directed inquiry and teacher learning

How students' choices and teachers' collaborative judgments influence the direction of inquiry.

-

Students can help determine the questions a class investigates, although the experience of directing an inquiry may be uncertain and uneven. In a Grade 7 Science and Technology project, students chose to investigate Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls and developed a public Red Dress exhibition. Their written reflections and interviews described a sense of ownership alongside difficulties making decisions, managing time, and collaborating. Some students recalled occasions when their ideas were overlooked by peers (Jao et al., 2026). These accounts lead me to ask how teachers recognize uneven participation and support students' autonomy without deciding the direction of an inquiry on their behalf.

-

The disciplinary relationships that teachers prepare can also influence students' experiences. In a Grade 8 interdisciplinary mathematics project, students described how connections to other subjects and the work of a teaching team shaped their understanding of mathematics. Some also found the approach unfamiliar in comparison with their previous lessons (Kiyani et al., 2025). I wonder how teachers can prepare useful disciplinary resources while leaving room for students to pursue connections that emerge during their work.

-

Teachers may be able to examine such decisions together. In a collaborative inquiry project involving educators from nine Ontario schools, participants developed and shared Grade 9 Applied Mathematics materials alongside professional learning activities. Interviews and reflections documented teachers' appreciation of the collaboration and their reports of further work together (Jao & McDougall, 2015). Jao's research team also describes ongoing projects examining cross-curricular competencies in student-directed STEAM inquiry and teacher-led professional development (Jao Research Team, n.d.). These project descriptions identify research aims rather than established findings.

-

My questions concern what teachers do with students' emerging ideas after an inquiry begins. I would like to examine how students and teachers negotiate the adequacy of scientific explanations, which contributions inform the next investigation, and how teachers might revisit those judgments through collaborative reflection.
